newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-RECORD-BREAKER CAMPESE STILL CHASING RAINBOWS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-RECORD-BREAKER CAMPESE STILL CHASING RAINBOWS.

text.p: As former Wallaby captain Nick Farr-Jones discovered when his squad gathered to chose their `player of the tour' in Britain in 1988, there are few rugby players to compare with David Campese.
Australians don't always respect the star in their midst, operating the "tall poppy" syndrome more ruthlessly than most.
But the poll underlined Campese's status as a man apart. "David was first," his skipper recalled, "Daylight was second."

With the odd well-publicised exception, the accolade sums up Campese's career. The modern history of Australian rugby would have been half as spectacular without him, and some might say even that is an understatement.

This week in Padova, the world's record test try-scorer reaches 100 international caps when the Wallabies face Italy, the land of his fathers. By the end of the year, he'll be gone for good and the rugby world will be a more predictable place.

With his 34th birthday on Monday, it should be time for Campese to chew reflectively on his achievements rather than indulge in any gnashing of teeth. This would, of course, alter the habit of a lifetime and he is not about to start.

"It's about time England got off their backsides and realised they are not the kings in rugby," he informed one British newspaper this week. "In the professional era, they're nobodies. Who'd go to watch the type of rugby they play?"

Welcome back to Europe, Campo the Diplomat. In his time he has accused South African players of arrogance and England captain Will Carling of "playing like a castrated bull". He also suggested `the only thing you're likely to get playing on the wing for England is chilblains'.

Good knock-about stuff, with at least a grain of truth in most of it, and central to any serious analysis of what motivates Campese. Virtually all his verbal darts are fired before a big game or major tour, barely any afterwards. In a tough game, no-one ever accused Campese of lacking courage although his team mates have not always appreciated his tact.
Former coach Bob Dwyer classified his winger as having `a loose wire between his brain and his mouth' but still devoted an entire chapter to the enigma in his autobiography.

"His instincts are always to do things which are above the ordinary," is Dwyer's assessment. "I have come to the conclusion his greatest single asset is courage...he has never wanted to be restricted by the fear of failure."

Who knows what would have happened to Campese had he been born an Englishman or stuck with rugby league, the code he played as a teenager in Canberra? No single man makes a rugby team, but how would Australia, even with the likes of Farr-Jones and Michael Lynagh, have fared since 1982 without his rapier skills and 64 test tries?

It was the voluble former Wallaby coach Alan Jones who styled him `the Bradman of Rugby', and Campese's peers have queued up to offer similar tributes. One of the most flattering was from the peerless Welsh fly-halfBarry John, who rated the winger's impact on the 1991 World Cup "as profound as that of Pele in the soccer World Cup of 1962".

The 1991 tournament will be forever remembered for the semifinal weekend in Dublin where Campese bamboozled New Zealand's defence with an angled run and touchdown to rank among the all-time greats, before conjuring an overhead pass which enabled Tim Horan to score another.

It fuelled Australia to the Webb Ellis trophy the following week at Twickenham against England, and another dig at Carling. "I read that, if England won the World Cup, Will Carling would become the first millionaire rugby player. That happened to me five years ago."

Yet even nine lucrative winters in Italy and assorted business interests in Sydney, including his own sports shop, have failed to prise Campese from rugby's embrace and he insists it is playing which continues to give his life its ultimate focus.

So despite the infamous fumble in 1989 which let in Lions' winger Ieuan Evans for the decisive try of the series, despite having scored only one international try -- against Canada -- in his last 11 tests dating back 17 months and despite being unceremoniously dropped last year, Campese can still be found chasing rainbows across foreign fields.
The only other man to top 100 international caps is French centre Philippe Sella with 111, but Campese insists dusk will finally descend on his test career at the end of this tour.
"When I stop playing I will be very upset," he once admitted. "I want to make sure there is nothing else I could have done."
